questions.prompt: Before opening any container in a certified Class II cabinet, which checks or actions belong in the pre-work step? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Pre-work establishes what may enter the cabinet and whether it is clean enough to enter.
feedback.solution: Inspect labels and closed cultures, reject expired medium and surface-disinfect items. Two cell lines must not be handled together, and UV does not replace chemical wiping.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Read both fresh-medium labels and reject the expired lot.
Bring both cell lines in so the second can be handled while the cabinet is already disinfected.
Inspect flask labels and appearance through the closed vessels.
Surface-disinfect every item before it enters the cabinet.
Use a UV lamp instead of wiping the interior because UV is faster.

questions.prompt: Which placements follow the clean-to-dirty arrangement used in the bench simulation? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Clean supplies, the open culture and dirty material should have separate positions.
feedback.solution: Clean supplies stay on the clean side, the target flask in the work centre, and turbid/waste material on the dirty side. Stacking and blocking grilles disturb airflow and shadow surfaces.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Fresh medium and sterile pipettes on the clean side
Target flask in the work centre
Turbid flask and waste container on the dirty side
Sterile pipettes stacked on the medium bottle to save space
A bottle placed across the front grille to keep it from rolling

questions.prompt: A colleague asks you to handle a different cell line in the same cabinet while your medium change is already set up. What is the correct aseptic decision?

feedback.hint: Cross-contamination and misidentification are the risks, not merely visible spills.
feedback.solution: Routine work should use only one cell line in the cabinet at a time. Separation, gloves or keeping a flask closed do not remove the cross-contamination risk.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Handle both lines if they are at opposite ends of the cabinet.
Handle only one cell line in the cabinet at a time and reschedule the second line.
Handle both lines if gloves are sanitized between them.
Handle both lines if the second line is not opened.

questions.prompt: You open a medium bottle and need both hands free for a moment. Where should the closure go?

feedback.hint: The surface that will touch the bottle must remain sterile.
feedback.solution: Hold the closure above the opening or place it upright on a disinfected surface. A face-down closure contacts a non-sterile surface and then contaminates the vessel.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Face down on the disinfected work surface
Held above the opening or upright on a disinfected surface
On the front ledge outside the cabinet
On top of the waste container

questions.prompt: In vertical unidirectional airflow, how should you approach an open flask during a transfer?

feedback.hint: Do not let hands or arms pass through the clean air above exposed material.
feedback.solution: Approach from the side and keep the body out of the airflow path. Reaching over an open container can shed particles into it.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: From the side, keeping your hands and arms out of the path over exposed product
Directly over the open flask so you can see the tip
Through the front opening with the sash fully raised
From behind the rear grille

questions.prompt: Which behaviours reduce contamination risk during an open transfer? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Aseptic technique controls particles, aerosols and sterile-to-sterile contact.
feedback.solution: Slow motion, fresh pipettes and sterile glove sanitization reduce risk. Talking over exposed product and rapid movements increase it, even if the flask is open for a shorter time.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Move slowly and gently
Use a fresh sterile pipette for each vessel or sample
Talk quietly while explaining the step over the open flask
Sanitize gloves with sterile alcohol before opening and after handling dirty material
Make rapid movements to minimize the time the flask is open

questions.prompt: A sterility-control schedule uses two valid incubation temperatures. What is the minimum total number of incubation days required within 20–35 °C? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: FDA process-simulation incubation requires at least 14 days within 20–35 °C.
feedback.solution: The minimum total is 14 valid days. A shorter schedule cannot be interpreted as a negative sterility result.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: When two incubation temperatures are used, what is the minimum number of days required at each temperature before the schedule satisfies the dual-temperature rule? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Each temperature must be held for at least one week, starting with the lower temperature.
feedback.solution: The minimum is 7 days at each temperature: at least 7 days at 20–25 °C first, then at least 7 days at 30–35 °C.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: According to the cell-culture guideline used in this lesson, how many different cell lines should be in the cabinet at the same time during routine work? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: The guideline recommends working with one culture at a time.
feedback.solution: Only one different cell line should be in the cabinet during routine work; two lines create cross-contamination and misidentification risk.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: A fresh-medium lot is labelled 0.22 µm filtered and remains clear after standard sterility incubation. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Filter pore size and visible turbidity are not the same evidence as a dedicated assay.
feedback.solution: Mycoplasmas can pass 0.22 µm filters and grow without turbidity; 0.1 µm filtration and routine dedicated testing address them. Standard sterility controls and clarity do not prove absence, and antibiotics are not reliable against mollicutes.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Mycoplasmas are typically about 0.15–0.3 µm and can pass a 0.22 µm filter.
A 0.1 µm filter is needed to retain mollicutes during sterilizing filtration.
No turbidity and a standard sterility control prove the lot is mycoplasma-free.
A dedicated mycoplasma assay is needed to detect mollicutes reliably.
Penicillin-streptomycin reliably eliminates all mollicutes.

questions.prompt: A culture may have been contaminated during a medium change. Why is adding penicillin-streptomycin not an acceptable rescue?

feedback.hint: Ask whether the antibiotic removes the contaminant or merely hides evidence of it.
feedback.solution: Antibiotics can delay or mask visible growth without sterilizing the culture, and mollicutes are often resistant. They do not repair an aseptic failure.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: It sterilizes the culture but changes the cells' phenotype.
It may mask visible growth without sterilizing the culture, and many mollicutes are resistant.
It is effective against mycoplasma but not bacteria.
It is forbidden in every cell-culture medium.

questions.prompt: A flask becomes visibly turbid after a medium change. Which responses are correct? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Containment prevents spread; testing identifies the problem; antibiotics do not solve it.
feedback.solution: Keep the turbid flask closed, contain it, decontaminate waste and surfaces, and follow your laboratory's testing/disposal procedure. Opening it in the clean workflow or adding antibiotics can spread or hide contamination.

modifications: Original aseptic-technique practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Keep the flask closed and contain it separately from clean cultures.
Open it in the same cabinet to identify the contaminant before disposal.
Decontaminate the waste and the cabinet before disposal and cleanup.
Submit or review dedicated contamination testing according to your procedure.
Add antibiotics and continue passaging until turbidity returns.

questions.prompt: You mix 15 µL of a cell suspension with 35 µL of trypan blue before loading the hemocytometer. What dilution factor must the count be multiplied by to give the concentration in the original suspension? Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: The factor is the total volume divided by the volume of cell suspension in it.
feedback.solution: (15 + 35)/15 = 50/15 = 3.33. Dividing dye by sample (35/15 = 2.33) is a ratio, not the dilution factor.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: A dense suspension is first diluted by adding 100 µL of it to 900 µL of medium. Ten microlitres of that are mixed with 10 µL of trypan blue. One Improved-Neubauer large square in chamber A holds 33 included unstained cells and one in chamber B holds 38. What is the viable-cell concentration of the original suspension, in units of 10⁶ cells/mL? Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: Multiply the two dilution factors, then use mean count × 10,000 × overall factor.
feedback.solution: Overall factor = (1000/100) × (20/10) = 10 × 2 = 20. Mean unstained = (33 + 38)/2 = 35.5, so 35.5 × 10,000 × 20 = 7.10 × 10⁶ cells/mL. Forgetting the medium step gives 0.710.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: After a 10 µL + 10 µL trypan-blue dilution, the large square counted in chamber A has 58 included unstained and 7 stained cells, and the one in chamber B has 63 unstained and 9 stained. What is the viable-cell concentration of the suspension, in units of 10⁶ cells/mL? Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: Use the mean included unstained count per large square, 10,000 per mL for a 0.1 µL square, and the dilution factor.
feedback.solution: Mean unstained = (58 + 63)/2 = 60.5; 60.5 × 10,000 × 2 = 1.21 × 10⁶ cells/mL. Adding the chambers without averaging gives 2.42, twice the true value.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: Two chambers of a trypan-blue count give 72 unstained and 11 stained included cells (chamber A) and 66 unstained and 13 stained (chamber B). What is the percent viability? Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: Viability is unstained over all included cells, using both chambers together.
feedback.solution: Unstained = 138, stained = 24, total = 162; 138/162 × 100 = 85.2%. Stained over unstained (24/138 = 17.4%) is neither viability nor the dead fraction.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: Chamber A gives 55 unstained and 9 stained included cells and chamber B gives 63 unstained and 12 stained. What is the Poisson relative counting uncertainty of the total-cell count, in percent? Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: Use 100/√N with N the number of cells in the count being reported; here all included cells from both chambers.
feedback.solution: N = 55 + 9 + 63 + 12 = 139; 100/√139 = 8.48%. Using 100/N gives 0.719%, far too small; for the viable count alone N = 118 and the uncertainty is 9.21%.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: A well-mixed suspension gives about 50 included cells per Improved-Neubauer large square. How many large squares must be counted in total for a Poisson relative counting uncertainty of 5% in the total count? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Invert 100/√N = 5 to find N, then divide by the cells per square.
feedback.solution: N = (100/5)² = 400 cells; 400/50 = 8 large squares, for example the four corners of each chamber. Twenty squares would come from mistaking √N for N.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: You count one large square using this lesson's convention: include cells touching the top or left boundary, exclude cells touching the bottom or right boundary, and let exclusion win at corners. Which decisions are correct? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Take the boundary decision first; a cell touching a bottom or right line is excluded whatever its colour.
feedback.solution: Top and left include, bottom and right exclude, and exclusion wins at a corner, so the top-right cell is excluded here and counted in the square to its right. The blue cell on the right line is excluded before its stain matters. A cell wholly inside needs only a stain decision.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: An unstained cell straddling the top line is included and tallied as unstained.
A blue cell straddling the right line is tallied as stained.
A cell sitting on the top-left corner, touching both of those lines, is included.
A cell sitting on the top-right corner, touching both of those lines, is included because it touches the top line.
A blue cell lying wholly inside the square needs only a stain decision, not a boundary decision.

questions.prompt: A trainee applies the boundary rule correctly to unstained cells but tallies every blue cell touching the bottom or right line as stained. Compared with a correct count, what happens to the two results?

feedback.hint: Ask which tally the extra cells enter, and which result uses that tally.
feedback.solution: The extra cells enter only the stained tally. Viable concentration uses only unstained cells, so it is unchanged; viability's denominator grows, so it falls. Boundary and stain decisions are separate.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Viable-cell concentration is unchanged and viability is biased low.
Viable-cell concentration is biased high and viability is unchanged.
Both results are biased low by the same percentage.
Neither result changes, because stained cells are not viable.

questions.prompt: Two chambers loaded from the same trypan-blue mixture give 31 and 74 included cells in their large squares. What is the best response?

feedback.hint: Compare the difference with the standard deviation expected for the difference of two Poisson counts.
feedback.solution: The difference should have a standard deviation of about √(a + b) = √105 ≈ 10.2; 43 is about 4.2 of those, which points to settling, mis-filling or bubbles rather than chance. Averaging hides a preparation error.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Do not average them: the difference of 43 is more than four times √(31 + 74) ≈ 10.2, beyond counting variation, so remix, reload both chambers and count again.
Average them to 52.5, since averaging two chambers cancels the error.
Keep the higher count, because cells are more often missed than double-counted.
Report both and widen the Poisson uncertainty to 100/√31 percent.

questions.prompt: A tube of suspension stood for ten minutes and both chambers were loaded from one aliquot taken near the surface without mixing. The chambers agree within 3%. What does the agreement show?

feedback.hint: Ask whether the error would differ between the two chambers or be shared by both.
feedback.solution: Replicates loaded from one unmixed aliquot share its systematic error: cells had settled away from the surface, so both counts are low together. Agreement measures precision, not accuracy; remix and resample.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Only that the two loadings were precise; both share the aliquot's bias, so the concentration is probably underestimated.
That the concentration is accurate to about 3%.
That settling did not occur, because settling would have made the chambers disagree.
That more squares are needed, because 3% is larger than the Poisson uncertainty.

questions.prompt: After a twofold trypan-blue dilution, one sample shows about 4 cells per large square and another about 300 overlapping cells per large square. Which plan is sound?

feedback.hint: Sparse fields give few cells and a large relative uncertainty; crowded fields cause boundary and stain mistakes.
feedback.solution: Four cells per square gives about 50% counting uncertainty per square, so count many more squares or concentrate. Three hundred overlapping cells are hard to assign and classify, so dilute and recount. Every change needs a new dilution factor.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Count many more squares, or concentrate the first sample; dilute the second further and recount, recalculating each dilution factor.
Count one square of each, because the dilution factor corrects for density.
Dilute the first sample further and concentrate the second.
Accept both counts, since Poisson uncertainty is the same at every density.

questions.prompt: A trypan-blue count of a culture gives 94% viability, made in buffered saline within three minutes of mixing. Which statements are supported? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Trypan-blue exclusion reports membrane integrity at one moment; ask which statements need a different assay.
feedback.solution: The test infers viability from membrane integrity, should be read in serum-free solution, and loses accuracy with prolonged dye exposure (Strober). It says nothing about future growth, contamination or phenotype.

modifications: Original cell-counting practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: About 94% of the counted cells excluded the dye, indicating intact membranes at the time of counting.
Counting in serum-free solution avoids serum proteins taking up the dye and misleading the count.
Leaving the cells in dye for 30 minutes before counting would be expected to lower the apparent viability.
The culture will proliferate normally after passaging.
The culture is free of mycoplasma and bacterial contamination.
The cells have the intended phenotype.

questions.prompt: You prepare 250 mL final volume of a synthetic medium containing 8% (v/v) serum from an undiluted serum stock. What volume of serum, in mL, is required? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Use V₁ = target volume fraction × final batch volume; the stock is 100% serum.
feedback.solution: C₁V₁ = C₂V₂ gives V₁ = (0.08 × 250 mL)/1.00 = 20 mL. The remaining 230 mL consists of basal medium and any other additions. Dividing 250 by 8 gives 31.25 and confuses a percentage with a dilution denominator; using 8 mL confuses percent with a 1:100 dilution.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: A 200 mM L-glutamine stock is used to prepare 400 mL final volume at 2 mM. What stock volume, in mL, is required? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Both concentrations are in mM, so V₁ = C₂V₂/C₁ needs no concentration-unit conversion.
feedback.solution: V₁ = (2 mM × 400 mL)/(200 mM) = 4 mL. This is also 400/100 mL because the stock is 100×. Using 400/200 = 2 mL ignores the 2 mM target; using 0.04 mL mistakes the 100-fold dilution for a 10,000-fold dilution.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: The simulation batch has a 500 mL final volume and contains 50 mL serum plus 5 mL of 100× glutamine stock. What basal-medium volume, in mL, makes the final total exactly 500 mL? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Subtract every supplement from the final batch volume, not from the starting basal volume.
feedback.solution: V_basal = 500 − 50 − 5 = 445 mL. Choosing 450 mL accounts for serum but forgets glutamine; adding 50 + 5 mL to 500 mL gives 555 mL and changes both final concentrations.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: For the synthetic volume-weighted approximation only, 445 mL basal medium at 290 mOsm/kg is mixed with 50 mL serum at 300 mOsm/kg and 5 mL glutamine stock at 400 mOsm/kg. What is the estimated final osmolality in mOsm/kg? Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.hint: Weight each component osmolality by its volume, sum the contributions, and divide by the 500 mL final volume.
feedback.solution: The estimate is (445 × 290 + 50 × 300 + 5 × 400)/500 = (129,050 + 15,000 + 2,000)/500 = 146,050/500 = 292.1 mOsm/kg, which is 292 mOsm/kg to three significant figures. An unweighted mean gives 330 and is wrong; real measurements supersede this explicitly approximate mixing rule.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

questions.prompt: Which statements correctly distinguish the roles of medium components and physical conditions? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Separate nutrients, buffer, indicator and solute concentration rather than treating them as one QC signal.
feedback.solution: Balanced salts and formulation-specific nutrients support the cells; bicarbonate and CO₂ jointly buffer pH; phenol red indicates rather than controls pH. Osmolality is not the same as pH. Serum-free does not necessarily mean supplement-free or fully defined, and phenol red does not supply the carbohydrate or amino-acid nutrients.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Basal formulations supply salts and formulation-specific nutrients such as carbohydrate, amino acids and vitamins.
Phenol red is the principal bicarbonate buffer and therefore fixes pH independently of CO₂.
Bicarbonate buffering depends on both dissolved bicarbonate and the surrounding CO₂ tension.
A correct pH measurement proves that osmolality is also correct.
Phenol red can indicate a pH shift, but it does not measure osmolality or establish sterility.

questions.prompt: An experiment is sensitive to variable, unidentified growth factors in serum. Which formulation strategy best addresses that specific problem while still requiring cell-line-specific evaluation?

feedback.hint: Look for known composition rather than merely a different source of an undefined mixture.
feedback.solution: A cell-line-appropriate chemically defined, serum-free formulation directly addresses unknown and variable serum components. Increasing serum does not remove them; “serum-free” alone does not prove fully defined; heat-inactivation changes selected serum activities but does not make the composition chemically defined.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Double the serum concentration so its unknown components remain constant relative to one another.
Use any product labelled serum-free, because every serum-free formulation is fully defined and supplement-free.
Evaluate a chemically defined, serum-free formulation for that cell line and experimental question.
Heat-inactivate the serum and assume all unidentified growth factors have been removed.

questions.prompt: You add 10 mL of a 100× supplement to 990 mL basal medium. Why is the nominal supplement strength 1× rather than approximately 1×?

feedback.hint: The dilution factor is final volume divided by stock volume.
feedback.solution: The final volume is 990 + 10 = 1,000 mL, so 100× × 10/1,000 = 1× exactly. Using 10/990 treats the basal volume as the denominator and yields an approximation; ignoring the added 10 mL makes every concentrated-stock calculation systematically inconsistent.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Because 100× divided by 100 mL of supplement gives 1×.
Because the stock volume is 1/100 of the final 1,000 mL: 100× × 10/1,000 = 1×.
Because a 100× stock always becomes 1× after adding any volume up to 100 mL.
Because only the basal-medium volume determines final concentration.

questions.prompt: Which handling decisions are appropriate for the lesson’s frozen concentrated L-glutamine supplement? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Preserve identity and lot history while limiting degradation and repeated freeze–thaw exposure.
feedback.solution: Use a documented frozen/cold aliquot, record lot and thaw details, and avoid repeated freeze–thaw cycles. L-glutamine in solution is not stable indefinitely; a room-temperature history is a suitability concern. Stabilized dipeptides are separate formulation choices and cannot be silently substituted without checking their instructions.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Select a single-use aliquot with a documented frozen/cold storage history and follow its thaw/mix instructions.
Keep the thawed stock at room temperature for convenience because cold glutamine never degrades.
Record the supplement lot and thaw details and avoid repeated freeze–thaw cycles.
Treat a stabilized glutamine-containing dipeptide as a distinct formulation choice rather than an undocumented substitution.

questions.prompt: A colleague proposes heat-inactivating every serum lot “to make any complete medium safe and defined.” What is the best evaluation?

feedback.hint: Ask what heat-inactivation is intended to change and which risks remain.
feedback.solution: Heat-inactivation is application-dependent, often used to reduce complement activity in selected immunological contexts; it is not needed routinely for every cell type. It neither guarantees sterility nor makes serum chemically defined, and heating can alter other serum properties. Follow the experimental and product-specific procedure.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Accept it: heat-inactivation makes any serum lot sterile, chemically defined and suitable for every cell line.
Reject the universal claim: use heat-inactivation only when the application calls for it, and retain aseptic handling, supplier controls and dedicated contamination testing.
Accept it only if the serum turns clear, because clarity demonstrates removal of mollicutes and viruses.
Reject all heat-inactivated serum because complement activity is required by every mammalian cell line.

questions.prompt: Which actions belong in the simulation’s heat-labile complete-medium filtration workflow? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: A sterilizing-grade pore label must be connected to compatible materials, aseptic assembly and an integrity result.
feedback.solution: Use the 0.22 µm protein-compatible filter with aseptic assembly and priming, then perform the device-supported bubble-point or pressure-hold check. Autoclaving can damage heat-labile components. Visual clarity is not an integrity test, and 0.22 µm filtration does not prove absence of mollicutes.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Select the 0.22 µm protein-compatible membrane and assemble the filter and sterile receiver aseptically.
Prime/pre-rinse according to the device procedure and perform a supported post-use integrity check.
Autoclave the complete serum- and glutamine-containing medium instead of filtering it.
Record filter identity/lot and the bubble-point or pressure-hold result with the batch.

questions.prompt: A 0.22 µm-filtered batch is clear, its filter-integrity check passes, and its standard sterility control has no visible growth after a valid schedule. What additional evidence is still needed for the mollicute risk?

feedback.hint: Separate mechanical retention and culturable growth from a dedicated assay for organisms that may pass the filter.
feedback.solution: Submit the dedicated mycoplasma lot test. Mollicutes may pass 0.22 µm filters and may not cause turbidity, so clarity, integrity and standard sterility incubation do not answer that specific question. A smaller nominal pore size would not replace the laboratory’s testing policy.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: No further evidence: the integrity pass proves every biological contaminant was removed.
No further evidence if the batch also contains penicillin-streptomycin.
A dedicated mycoplasma test, because filtration and visible growth do not reliably detect or remove this risk.
Only another visual inspection, because mollicutes always produce turbidity within 24 hours.

questions.prompt: Which decisions complete a traceable QC and storage workflow for the synthetic batch? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Release requires traceability, valid incubation and the independent assay; storage does not rescue missing evidence.
feedback.solution: The label/record links formulation, cell line, dates, batch and component lots; aliquots are stored at 2–8 °C protected from light; the batch remains quarantined pending required QC. Clarity alone is not release evidence. Aliquot allocation cannot exceed recovered volume, and the 14-day expiry is a simulation choice rather than a universal shelf life.

modifications: Original media-preparation practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and values; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Label the formulation, intended cell line, preparation/expiry dates and batch ID, and link basal, serum, glutamine and filter lots.
Release immediately if the filtrate is clear, before the sterility schedule and mycoplasma result.
Store traceably labelled aliquots at 2–8 °C protected from light and keep the batch quarantined until required QC is acceptable.
Allocate any number of 50 mL aliquots because filtration creates additional volume.
Account for QC and aliquot volumes, and treat the printed 14-day expiry as a synthetic teaching convention.

questions.prompt: A synthetic adherent culture is 78% confluent with expected morphology, clear medium and 93% dye-exclusion viability. Under this lesson's simulation rule, which disposition is appropriate?

feedback.hint: Use the declared 70–85% teaching window, but keep the evidence domains separate.
feedback.solution: The culture lies within the synthetic 70–85% routine window, so routine passaging is appropriate in the scenario. The 93% result describes membrane integrity at counting time; it does not prove identity or sterility, and 95% is the separate refusal scenario.

modifications: Original passaging practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Proceed with the routine passage workflow while continuing to monitor the culture.
Discard it solely because routine passaging is permitted only below 50% confluence.
Treat the viability result as proof of identity and sterility before passaging.
Delay passage until the culture reaches 95% confluence.

questions.prompt: Which actions support a representative, viable harvest in the lesson's adherent workflow? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: Separate substrate detachment from mixing, and consider both reagent carry-over and exposure time.
feedback.solution: The wash reduces inhibitors of dissociation; detachment is observed before neutralization; and resuspension makes the count representative. Longer exposure is not always better, suspension cells do not attach to the medium, and no substrate-detachment step is needed for them.

modifications: Original passaging practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Wash with calcium- and magnesium-free balanced salt solution before adding the dissociation reagent.
Observe detachment and stop or dilute dissociation activity with complete medium at the appropriate step.
Extend dissociation until every cell is rounded, regardless of elapsed time.
Resuspend to a representative single-cell suspension before sampling for the count.
Add the dissociation reagent to a suspension culture to detach it from the medium.

questions.prompt: A suspension culture contains 1.6 × 10⁶ viable cells/mL. It will be passaged to 0.4 × 10⁶ viable cells/mL in 20 mL. Which plan is conceptually and arithmetically correct?

feedback.hint: Required cells are C₂V₂; fresh medium is final volume minus the culture inoculum, and no substrate detachment is needed.
feedback.solution: Required viable cells = 0.4 × 10⁶ × 20 = 8.0 × 10⁶. Culture volume = (8.0 × 10⁶)/(1.6 × 10⁶) = 5.0 mL, so fresh medium = 20 − 5 = 15 mL. Suspension cells need no detachment reagent; 8 mL confuses a volume fraction with cell conservation.

modifications: Original passaging practice developed with substantial AI assistance; synthetic scenario and data; no external problem, dataset or figure imported.

options: Use an enzyme to detach the cells, then add 20 mL medium to 5 mL culture.
Mix and count a representative sample, transfer 5 mL culture, and add 15 mL fresh medium.
Transfer 8 mL culture and add 12 mL medium because 8/20 = 0.4.
Transfer 0.5 mL culture and add 19.5 mL medium because 1.6/0.4 = 4 and 20/4 = 5.

questions.prompt: A harvested suspension contains 1.21 × 10⁶ viable cells/mL. How many millilitres are needed per flask to seed 5.00 × 10⁵ viable cells? Keep full precision in intermediate calculations. Enter the number only, to three significant figures.

feedback.solution: V = (5.00 × 10⁵ cells)/(1.21 × 10⁶ cells/mL) ≈ 0.413 mL = 4.13 × 10⁻¹ mL to three significant figures. Using total rather than viable cells would make the inoculum too small.

questions.prompt: At the start of a culture interval there are 1.815 × 10⁶ viable cells (N0); at harvest there are 7.26 × 10⁶ (Nf). What is the PDL increment, log₂(Nf/N0)? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Take the ratio first, then the base-two logarithm; passage number is not the same as PDL.
feedback.solution: Nf/N0 = 7.26/1.815 = 4. PDL increment = log₂4 = log₁₀4/log₁₀2 = 2. Each of the two doublings multiplies cell number by two; this does not mean two separate passage events.

questions.prompt: A culture's previous cumulative PDL is 18.00. During the next interval, N0 = 1.25 × 10⁶ and Nf = 5.00 × 10⁶. What is the new cumulative PDL? Enter the number only.

feedback.hint: Add the interval's log₂(Nf/N0) increment to the previous cumulative value.
feedback.solution: Nf/N0 = 5.00/1.25 = 4, so the increment is log₂4 = 2. New cumulative PDL = 18.00 + 2 = 20. Adding four instead of two confuses the fold increase with its base-two logarithm.

questions.prompt: A planner needs 5.0 × 10⁵ viable cells but divides that target by total-cell concentration rather than viable-cell concentration. Viability is below 100%, and all volumes are transferred as calculated. What is the effect?

feedback.hint: Compare the denominator in N/C when total concentration exceeds viable concentration.
feedback.solution: Total concentration = viable concentration/viability fraction, so it is larger when viability is below 100%. Dividing by the larger number gives a smaller inoculum and too few viable cells. The correct calculation uses viable-cell concentration and still accounts for the dilution.

questions.prompt: Which entries or interpretations belong in a sound passage review? Select all that apply.

feedback.hint: A traceable record preserves measurements and provenance; it does not turn indirect evidence into identity evidence.
feedback.solution: Raw counts, dilution, yields, target/final volumes, dates, vessels and reagent lots make the calculation auditable. Passage events and PDL are distinct. Repeated subculture can change characteristics, but passage number alone does not prove drift and dye exclusion does not authenticate a line; later authentication review is required.
